newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Security tightens ahead of Cyprus's peace concert.
newsitem.headline: Security tightens ahead of Cyprus's peace concert.

text.p: Roadblocks, rows of barbed wire snaking across streets, bright yellow police ribbons and scores of police was the untypical picture in Cyprus's capital Nicosia on Monday.
Police mounted a massive security operation in the capital to ensure that a United Nations-sponsored bicommunal peace concert scheduled to take place later on Monday remained peaceful.
"We have taken all indicative security measures and all access points to the concert venue are controlled," Cyprus police spokesman Glafcos Xenos told Reuters.
Pop stars Burak Kut of Turkey and Sakis Rouvas of Greece were to sing to a crowd of around 5,000 young people in the U.N.-controlled no-mans-land of the capital.
The aim was to break the ice, or begin to thaw it, between the youth of the island's two communities separated by years of enmity and mistrust.
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in an invasion sparked by a brief Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
The concert has taken on a political meaning in the face of angry reactions from various groups on both sides of the divide.

A far-right Turkish nationalist group drove around the Turkish section of Nicosia on Monday afternoon with loudspeakers publicising a protest meeting against the concert which they were to hold during the evening at their headquarters.
In the south, some Greek Cypriot groups who see the concert as an act of defeatism and an attempt to peddle Turkish propaganda plan a protest just a mile (two km) away from the concert venue.
Turkey's Kut arrived in northern Cyprus on Sunday and was met by fans with flowers. He told reporters that the aim of the concert was to deliver a message of peace and friendship.
"I believe that not just countries but individuals too should refrain from being angry with each other," he said.

Rouvas's arrival in Cyprus, in contrast, was kept a secret. He appeared around midday on Monday in Nicosia looking conspicuous in dark sunglasses along with the rest of his entourage. He didn't talk to reporters. He just smiled.
Turkish Cypriots snapped up all 3,000 free tickets allocated to their community.
But the chance to see Rouvas -- one of Greece's hottest rock stars -- for free did not appear to appeal to many Greek Cypriots.
The United Nations were forced to expand their ticket distribution network to allocate their tickets, and still only managed to get rid of 2,000 of the 3,000 on offer.
